os-fifo-page-faults.title: Page Faults under FIFO Replacement
os-fifo-page-faults.description:
A process touches pages in the order given by `refs`. Physical memory has `frames` page frames, all
initially empty. On a reference to a page that is not loaded, a **page fault** occurs; if no frame is
free, the page that has been in memory **longest** (first in, first out) is evicted.

Return the number of page faults.

**Example:** `refs = [1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2], frames = 3` → `4`
(faults on 1, 2, 3; hit on 1; fault on 4 evicts page 1; hit on 2).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(refs) ≤ 10^5`, `0 ≤ frames ≤ 10^4`. With zero frames every reference faults.

guide.prereqs: Paging and page faults (memory lessons), `set` and `collections.deque`.
guide.intuition: FIFO only cares about *load order*. A hit changes nothing at all — that is exactly what makes it different from LRU, and exactly why it can evict a heavily used page.
hints: You need two views of memory: fast membership (a set) and age order (a queue).
On a hit do nothing. On a fault with full memory, pop the queue's left end and remove that page from the set.
Handle `frames == 0` up front: every reference is a fault and there is nothing to evict.
guide.brute_force: Keep the loaded pages in a plain list: `p in list` is O(frames) and `pop(0)` is O(frames), giving O(n·frames). Correct, but too slow for 60,000 references and hundreds of frames.
guide.approach:
1. `mem = set()`, `order = deque()`, `faults = 0`.
2. For each page: if in `mem`, continue. Otherwise count a fault; if `len(mem) == frames`, evict `order.popleft()`; add the page to both structures.

**Dry run** `[1,2,3,1,4,2]`, 3 frames: load 1, 2, 3 (3 faults, queue 1→2→3). 1 hits, queue unchanged. 4 faults, evicts 1 (queue 2→3→4). 2 hits. Total 4.
guide.complexity: O(n) time with O(1) work per reference; O(frames) space.
guide.pitfalls: Moving a page to the back of the queue on a hit (that is LRU). Returning the count of distinct pages, which ignores re-faults after eviction. Crashing on zero frames.
guide.follow_up: Run the reference string `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5` with 3 and then 4 frames. More memory gives *more* faults — Belady's anomaly, impossible for stack algorithms such as LRU.

os-lru-page-faults.title: Page Faults under LRU Replacement
os-lru-page-faults.description:
Same setting as FIFO paging, but on a fault with no free frame the victim is the page whose **most
recent use lies furthest in the past** (least recently used).

Given the reference string `refs` and the number of frames, return the number of page faults.

**Example:** `refs = [1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 2], frames = 3` → `5`
(4 evicts page 2, the least recently used, so the final reference to 2 faults again).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(refs) ≤ 10^5`, `0 ≤ frames ≤ 10^4`.

guide.prereqs: FIFO page replacement, `collections.OrderedDict` (or a dict of last-use times).
guide.intuition: The recent past is the best cheap predictor of the near future: a page untouched for a long time probably belongs to a phase the program has left. Keep pages ordered by last use; the stale end is the victim.
hints: Start from FIFO and ask: what must change on a *hit*?
An `OrderedDict` keeps insertion order; `move_to_end(page)` refreshes a page in O(1).
Evict with `popitem(last=False)` — the entry that has gone longest without being refreshed.
guide.brute_force: Store `last_used[page] = index` and on each eviction scan all loaded pages for the smallest value: O(frames) per fault, O(n·frames) worst case. Simple and worth writing first.
guide.approach:
1. `mem = OrderedDict()`.
2. Hit → `mem.move_to_end(p)`. Miss → fault; if full, `mem.popitem(last=False)`; then `mem[p] = True`.

**Dry run** `[1,2,3,1,4,2]`, 3 frames: after 1,2,3 the order is 1,2,3 (3 faults). Hit on 1 → 2,3,1. 4 faults and evicts 2 → 3,1,4. 2 faults and evicts 3. Total 5.
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(frames) space.
guide.pitfalls: Confusing LRU with LFU (least *frequently* used) — the second wrong solution does exactly that. Forgetting to refresh on a hit turns the code into FIFO.
guide.follow_up: True LRU needs work on *every* memory reference, which hardware cannot afford; that is why real kernels approximate it with reference bits (clock, aging).

os-optimal-page-faults.title: Page Faults under the Optimal (Belady) Policy
os-optimal-page-faults.description:
The optimal replacement policy looks into the future: on a fault with no free frame it evicts the
loaded page whose **next use is furthest away** (or that is never used again). It cannot be built in a
real system, but it gives the lower bound every practical algorithm is measured against.

Return the number of page faults for `refs` with `frames` frames.

**Example:** `refs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], frames = 3` → `7`

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(refs) ≤ 10^5`, `0 ≤ frames ≤ 10^4`. Aim for better than O(n · frames).

guide.prereqs: FIFO and LRU fault counting, heaps, precomputing 'next occurrence' arrays with a right-to-left scan.
guide.intuition: If you must throw something away, throw away what you will need last. An exchange argument shows no other choice can produce fewer faults: swapping any other victim for the farthest-future one never makes things worse.
hints: For every position `i` precompute `nxt[i]`, the index of the next reference to the same page (or infinity). One backward pass with a dict does it.
Each loaded page has a current 'next use'. The victim is the page with the largest one — a max-heap.
When a page is hit its next use changes. Push the new value and let stale heap entries be discarded lazily when popped.
guide.brute_force: On each fault, for every loaded page scan forward through `refs` to find its next use. O(n · frames · n) in the worst case; fine for classroom-sized strings, hopeless for 50,000 references.
guide.approach:
1. Backward pass → `nxt`.
2. `cur[page]` = its next-use index. Heap of `(-next_use, page)`.
3. For each reference: if absent, fault; if full, pop until the entry matches `cur` (not stale), delete that page. Then set `cur[p] = nxt[i]` and push.

**Dry run** `[1,2,3,4,1,2,5,...]`, 3 frames: after 1,2,3 the next uses are 4,5,9. Page 4 faults → evict 3 (next use 9 is farthest). 1 and 2 hit. 5 faults: next uses are 1→7, 2→8, 4→10 → evict 4. Continuing gives 7 faults in total.
guide.complexity: O(n log n) time (each reference pushes once; each entry is popped at most once), O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Treating 'never used again' as distance 0 instead of infinity. Forgetting to update a page's next use on a hit. Using stale heap entries. Believing this can be implemented in an OS — it needs the future.
guide.follow_up: Compare the three counts on the same string: optimal ≤ LRU always, and LRU's fault count never rises when frames are added (it is a *stack algorithm*).

os-clock-page-faults.title: Clock (Second Chance) Replacement
os-clock-page-faults.description:
Simulate the **clock** page replacement algorithm.

Memory is a circular array of `frames` slots, all empty, and a hand that starts at slot 0. Every loaded
page has a reference bit `R`.

- **Hit:** set the page's `R` to 1. The hand does not move.
- **Fault:** look at the slot under the hand. While it holds a page with `R = 1`, clear the bit and
  advance the hand (wrapping around). When the hand rests on an empty slot or a page with `R = 0`,
  put the new page there (evicting the old occupant, if any), set its `R` to 1 and advance the hand one slot.

Return `[faults, slots]` where `slots` is the final content of the frames in slot order, using `-1` for
an empty slot.

**Example:** `refs = [1, 2, 3, 1, 4], frames = 3` → `[4, [4, 2, 3]]`
(when 4 arrives all three bits are 1; the hand clears them in one full circle and replaces page 1 at slot 0).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(refs) ≤ 10^5`, `1 ≤ frames ≤ 10^4`, page numbers are non-negative.

guide.prereqs: FIFO replacement, the hardware-maintained referenced bit, modular arithmetic for circular arrays.
guide.intuition: Clock is FIFO with mercy. The hand visits pages in load order, but a page that has been used since the hand last passed gets its bit cleared and one more lap of life. Only pages that stay untouched for a whole revolution are evicted.
hints: Keep three things: `slots` (page per frame), `rbit` (per frame) and a dict from page to slot for O(1) hits.
The fault loop is: while the slot under the hand is occupied *and* its bit is 1, clear and step.
The sweep always terminates: after at most one full circle every bit is 0.
guide.brute_force: Implement second chance literally as a queue: pop the oldest page; if its bit is set, clear it and append it to the tail; repeat. Same victims, but each move shuffles list elements, whereas the circular array just moves an index.
guide.approach:
1. On a hit set the bit; nothing else.
2. On a fault sweep the hand as described, replace, set bit, advance.

**Dry run** `[1,2,3,1,4]`, 3 frames: 1, 2, 3 fill slots 0–2 with R=1; hand is back at 0. Hit on 1. Fault on 4: slot 0 R=1 → clear, slot 1 → clear, slot 2 → clear, back at slot 0 with R=0 → replace page 1. Slots `[4,2,3]`, hand at 1, faults 4.
guide.complexity: Amortised O(1) per reference in practice; a single fault can sweep O(frames) slots, so the worst case is O(n · frames). Space O(frames).
guide.pitfalls: Moving the hand on a hit. Loading the new page with R=0 (it would be evicted immediately by the next sweep — second wrong solution). Forgetting to delete the evicted page from the lookup dict. Not advancing the hand after placement.
guide.follow_up: Add a modified bit and prefer clean pages (the enhanced clock used by many kernels), or add a second hand a fixed distance behind the first.

os-aging-page-replacement.title: Aging Counters and Victim Selection
os-aging-page-replacement.description:
The **aging** algorithm approximates LRU in software. Every page in memory has a `bits`-bit counter,
initially 0. At each clock tick, for every page:

1. shift its counter right by one bit,
2. put the page's referenced bit (1 if the page was touched during that tick, else 0) into the leftmost position.

`ticks[t]` lists the pages referenced during tick `t` (possibly with repeats). Pages are numbered
`0 .. pages-1` and all of them stay in memory.

Return `[counters, victim]`: the final counter of each page, and the page that would be evicted now —
the one with the smallest counter (lowest page number on ties).

**Example:** `ticks = [[0, 2], [0], [1]], pages = 3, bits = 4` → `[[6, 8, 2], 2]`
(page 0: `1000 → 1100 → 0110`; page 1: `0000 → 0000 → 1000`; page 2: `1000 → 0100 → 0010`).

**Constraints:** `1 ≤ pages ≤ 2000`, `1 ≤ bits ≤ 32`, `0 ≤ len(ticks) ≤ 2000`.

guide.prereqs: Bit shifts and masks, the referenced bit, why exact LRU is too expensive (page replacement lesson).
guide.intuition: Read a counter as a history string, newest tick on the left. Comparing counters as integers compares histories lexicographically: a page touched in the latest tick beats every page that was not, no matter how busy the others were long ago.
hints: Every page ages every tick — including the ones that were not referenced.
The new bit goes in at position `bits - 1`: `counter = (counter >> 1) | (R << (bits - 1))`.
Convert each tick's list to a set first so duplicate references inside one tick count once.
guide.brute_force: Store each page's history as a list of 0/1 values, prepend the new bit each tick, truncate to `bits`, and convert to an integer at the end. Same answer with far more allocation.
guide.approach:
1. `counters = [0] * pages`, `top = 1 << (bits - 1)`.
2. For each tick: build the touched set; shift every counter right; OR in `top` for touched pages.
3. Victim = argmin of `(counter, page)`.

**Dry run** from the example with 4 bits: tick 0 touches 0 and 2 → `[8,0,8]`. Tick 1 touches 0 → `[12,0,4]`. Tick 2 touches 1 → `[6,8,2]`. Smallest is page 2.
guide.complexity: O(ticks × pages + total references) time, O(pages) space.
guide.pitfalls: Shifting left and inserting at the right (first wrong solution) — that makes *old* references the most significant. Ageing only the referenced pages (second wrong solution), so idle pages never decay. Counting a page twice in one tick.
guide.follow_up: Aging differs from true LRU in two ways: it cannot order two references inside one tick, and its memory is only `bits` ticks long. Construct inputs where each limitation picks a different victim from LRU.

os-working-set-size.title: Working Set Size over Time
os-working-set-size.description:
The **working set** $w(k, t)$ of a process is the set of distinct pages among its most recent `k`
memory references at time `t`.

Given a reference string `refs` and a window `k ≥ 1`, return a list `out` with `out[t]` = the number
of distinct pages among `refs[max(0, t-k+1) .. t]` (the current reference is included).

**Example:** `refs = [1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 3, 4], k = 3` → `[1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2]`

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(refs) ≤ 2·10^5`, `1 ≤ k ≤ 2·10^5`. An O(n·k) solution is too slow.

guide.prereqs: Sliding-window technique with a frequency map; locality of reference and the working-set model (memory lessons).
guide.intuition: As the window slides by one position, exactly one reference enters and at most one leaves. Track how many times each page occurs inside the window; the number of keys with a non-zero count is the working set size.
hints: Recomputing `len(set(window))` every step costs O(k) each time. What changes between consecutive windows?
Use a dict of counts. Add the new page; if the window is now longer than `k`, decrement the page falling off the left edge.
Delete a key when its count reaches zero so that `len(count)` is the answer.
guide.brute_force: `[len(set(refs[max(0,t-k+1):t+1])) for t in range(n)]` — clear and correct, O(n·k). Use it to test the fast version on random inputs.
guide.approach:
1. For index `t`: `count[refs[t]] += 1`.
2. If `t >= k`: the element `refs[t-k]` leaves; decrement and delete at zero.
3. Append `len(count)`.

**Dry run** `[1,2,1,3,3,3,4]`, k=3: windows are [1], [1,2], [1,2,1], [2,1,3], [1,3,3], [3,3,3], [3,3,4] → sizes 1,2,2,3,2,1,2.
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(min(k, distinct pages)) space.
guide.pitfalls: Off-by-one on the window edge (the first wrong solution keeps k+1 references). Decrementing without deleting, then counting keys with zero counts. Returning the cumulative number of distinct pages.
guide.follow_up: Real kernels define the window in *virtual time* (CPU time used by the process) and approximate it with a referenced bit plus a time-of-last-use field — the WSClock algorithm.

os-two-level-translation.title: Two-level Page Table Translation
os-two-level-translation.description:
Translate a virtual address with a **two-level page table**.

A virtual address is split, from most to least significant bits, into:

`| directory index | table index (pt_bits bits) | offset (offset_bits bits) |`

- `page_dir` is a list. `page_dir[d]` is either `None` (no second-level table) or a list — the second-level table.
- An entry `table[t]` is either `None` (page not present) or the physical **frame number**.
- An index beyond the end of a list also counts as "not mapped".

Return the physical address `frame * 2**offset_bits + offset`, or `-1` if the translation faults.

**Example:** `vaddr = 0x1234, page_dir = [None, [None, None, 7]], offset_bits = 8, pt_bits = 4`
→ offset `0x34`, table index `2`, directory index `1`, frame 7 → `7*256 + 0x34 = 1844`.

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ vaddr < 2^48`, `1 ≤ offset_bits ≤ 16`, `1 ≤ pt_bits ≤ 12`.
os-two-level-translation.starter:
def translate(vaddr, page_dir, offset_bits, pt_bits):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Binary and hexadecimal, shifts and masks, the paging lesson (virtual page number, offset, frame number, multilevel tables).
guide.intuition: Paging never changes the offset — it only swaps the page number for a frame number. A two-level table simply performs that swap in two hops, so that unused regions of the address space cost one `None` in the directory instead of a whole table.
hints: Peel fields off from the right: mask the low `offset_bits`, shift, mask the next `pt_bits`, shift; what remains is the directory index.
Check each level for 'index out of range' and for `None` before descending.
Frame number 0 is a perfectly valid frame. Test with `is None`, not truthiness.
guide.brute_force: Convert the address to a binary string, pad it, and slice out the fields by character positions. It works, and is a reasonable way to check the bit-twiddling version, but it is slow and breaks easily on padding.
guide.approach:
1. `offset = v & (2^o - 1)`; `t = (v >> o) & (2^p - 1)`; `d = v >> (o + p)`.
2. Fault if `d` is out of range or `page_dir[d] is None`; fault if `t` is out of range or the entry is `None`.
3. Answer `(frame << o) | offset`.

**Dry run** `0x1234`, o=8, p=4: offset `0x34`; `0x12 & 0xF = 2`; `0x12 >> 4 = 1`. `page_dir[1][2] = 7` → `0x734 = 1844`.
guide.complexity: O(1) time and space — which is the point: translation cost depends on the number of levels, not on the size of the address space.
guide.pitfalls: Treating frame 0 as 'not present' (first wrong solution). Swapping the two index fields (second wrong solution). Adding instead of OR-ing is fine here, but multiplying the frame by the page *count* rather than the page *size* is a classic slip.
guide.follow_up: x86-64 uses four levels of 9 bits each over a 12-bit offset (48-bit addresses), and five levels on newer CPUs. Generalise the function to a list of field widths.

os-tlb-simulation.title: TLB Hit/Miss Simulation
os-tlb-simulation.description:
A translation lookaside buffer caches recent page-number → frame translations. Simulate a fully
associative TLB with `tlb_size` entries and **LRU** replacement.

For each virtual address in `addresses`, its virtual page number is `address // page_size`. If the
page number is in the TLB it is a hit (and becomes the most recently used entry); otherwise it is a
miss and the page number is inserted, evicting the least recently used entry if the TLB is full.

Return `[hits, misses]`.

**Example:** `addresses = [0, 4, 4096, 8, 8192, 4100], page_size = 4096, tlb_size = 2` → `[2, 4]`
(page sequence `0 0 1 0 2 1`: miss, hit, miss, hit, miss — evicting page 1 — and then page 1 misses again, evicting page 0).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(addresses) ≤ 10^5`, `page_size ≥ 1`, `0 ≤ tlb_size ≤ 4096`.

guide.prereqs: LRU page-fault counting (same data structure), the role of the TLB in address translation.
guide.intuition: The TLB does not care about bytes, only about pages: thousands of accesses inside one page are one entry. So first reduce each address to its page number, then run an ordinary LRU cache simulation.
hints: Compute `vpn = address // page_size` before anything else.
An `OrderedDict` gives O(1) lookup, refresh (`move_to_end`) and eviction (`popitem(last=False)`).
A zero-entry TLB can never hit; make sure you do not try to evict from an empty structure.
guide.brute_force: Keep the entries in a list ordered by recency: on a hit remove and append; on a miss pop index 0 when full. O(tlb_size) per access — acceptable for 64 entries, but the OrderedDict is cleaner.
guide.approach:
For each address: page number; hit → count and refresh; miss → count, evict oldest if full, insert.

**Dry run** pages `0 0 1 0 2 1`, 2 entries: miss(0); hit; miss(1) → {0,1}; hit(0) → order 1,0; miss(2) evicts 1 → {0,2}; miss(1) evicts 0. Result `[2, 4]`.
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(tlb_size) space.
guide.pitfalls: Caching raw addresses rather than page numbers (second wrong solution). Using FIFO eviction (first wrong solution). Dividing by the number of offset *bits* instead of the page size.
guide.follow_up: Compute the effective access time: with hit ratio h, TLB lookup time e, and memory access time m, a one-level table costs `h(e+m) + (1-h)(e+2m)`.

os-first-fit.title: First-fit Memory Allocation
os-first-fit.description:
Free memory is described by `holes`, the sizes of the free regions in address order. Requests arrive
one at a time. With **first fit**, each request is carved from the *first* hole (lowest index) that is
large enough; the hole shrinks by the request size (a hole of size 0 stays in the list and is simply useless).

Return a list giving, for each request, the index of the hole used, or `-1` if no hole can satisfy it.

**Example:** `holes = [100, 500, 200, 300, 600], requests = [212, 417, 112, 426]` → `[1, 4, 1, -1]`

**Constraints:** up to 2000 holes and 2000 requests, sizes are positive integers.

guide.prereqs: The memory lesson on free-list management (first fit, next fit, best fit, worst fit).
guide.intuition: First fit is the laziest possible search: walk the free list from the start and stop at the first region that works. Its virtue is speed; its cost is a clutter of small leftovers near the front of memory.
hints: Copy the hole list so you can shrink holes without mutating the caller's data.
Python's `for ... else` runs the `else` branch only when the loop did not `break` — ideal for 'nothing fitted'.
A hole exactly equal to the request is usable; compare with `>=`.
guide.brute_force: The direct double loop *is* the algorithm: O(holes) per request. There is nothing slower worth writing.
guide.approach:
For each request scan holes left to right; at the first `free[i] >= r` subtract and record `i`; otherwise record `-1`.

**Dry run** holes `[100,500,200,300,600]`: 212 → hole 1 (288 left). 417 → holes 0–3 too small (100, 288, 200, 300), hole 4 fits (183 left). 112 → hole 1 (176 left). 426 → nothing ≥ 426 → -1.
guide.complexity: O(R · H) time, O(H) extra space.
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting to shrink the hole (second wrong solution). Picking the tightest hole (that is best fit — first wrong solution). Note the last request fails although 100+176+200+300+183 = 959 bytes are free in total: that is **external fragmentation**.
guide.follow_up: Implement *next fit*, which resumes the search where the previous one stopped, and compare how the holes end up distributed.

os-best-fit.title: Best-fit Memory Allocation
os-best-fit.description:
Same model as first fit: `holes` are free-region sizes in address order and each request shrinks the
hole it is carved from. With **best fit** the allocator picks the **smallest hole that is still large
enough**; if several holes tie, it uses the one with the lowest index.

Return the list of hole indices used (or `-1` for requests that cannot be satisfied).

**Example:** `holes = [100, 500, 200, 300, 600], requests = [212, 417, 112, 426]` → `[3, 1, 2, 4]`

**Constraints:** up to 2000 holes and 2000 requests, positive sizes.

guide.prereqs: First-fit allocation (previous problem).
guide.intuition: Best fit tries to preserve large holes for large future requests by always spending the tightest region. The side effect is a litter of tiny slivers too small for anyone, which is why it is not automatically better than first fit.
hints: You must look at every hole for each request — there is no early exit.
Track the index of the best candidate so far; replace it only when the new hole is strictly smaller.
Strict `<` (not `<=`) is what implements 'lowest index on ties'.
guide.brute_force: Sort candidate holes by size for every request (O(H log H) each). A single linear scan for the minimum does the same in O(H).
guide.approach:
For each request: scan all holes, remember the smallest one with `size >= r`, subtract, record.

**Dry run** `[100,500,200,300,600]`: 212 → candidates 500, 300, 600 → hole 3 (88 left). 417 → 500 or 600 → hole 1 (83 left). 112 → 200 or 600 → hole 2 (88 left). 426 → hole 4 (174 left). Every request succeeds here, where first fit failed the last one.
guide.complexity: O(R · H) time, O(H) space. A balanced tree keyed by size would give O(log H) per request.
guide.pitfalls: Breaking at the first fit. Using `<=` and so preferring the *highest* index on ties. Assuming best fit always wastes less memory — simulations show it often leaves more unusable fragments than first fit.
guide.follow_up: Try *worst fit* (always the largest hole) and count failed requests for the same random workload under all three policies.

os-buddy-allocator.title: Buddy System Allocator
os-buddy-allocator.description:
Implement a **binary buddy allocator** managing `total` units of memory (`total` is a power of two).
The smallest block is 1 unit.

`ops` is a list of operations:

- `["alloc", size]` — round `size` up to the next power of two `b`. Find the smallest free block of
  size `≥ b` (lowest address among blocks of that size). Split it in halves repeatedly — always keeping
  the **lower** half and freeing the upper half — until it has size `b`. Return its start address, or
  `-1` if no free block is large enough.
- `["free", addr]` — release the allocated block that starts at `addr`. While the freed block's
  buddy (the other half of the block they were split from) is also completely free, merge the two.
  Return the size of the resulting free block. If `addr` is not the start of an allocated block, return `-1`.

Return the list of results.

**Example:** `total = 16, ops = [["alloc",3],["alloc",2],["free",0],["alloc",8],["free",4],["free",8]]`
→ `[0, 4, 4, 8, 8, 16]`

**Constraints:** `1 ≤ total ≤ 2^20`, `1 ≤ size`, up to 20,000 operations.

guide.prereqs: Powers of two and XOR, free lists, internal vs external fragmentation. The Linux case-study lesson describes where the kernel uses this allocator.
guide.intuition: Restricting block sizes to powers of two makes two hard things trivial. Splitting is halving. And the partner a block may merge with is fixed by arithmetic: for a block of size `s` at address `a`, the buddy lives at `a XOR s`. No searching of neighbours is ever needed.
hints: Keep one set of free addresses per block size (`free[1]`, `free[2]`, `free[4]`, …) and a dict `used[addr] = size`.
Allocation: round up, climb to the first size with a free block, take the lowest address, then split down, adding each upper half to its free set.
Freeing: loop while `addr ^ size` is in `free[size]` — remove the buddy, keep the lower address, double the size.
guide.brute_force: Model memory as an array of `total` cells and search for aligned free runs on each allocation, re-scanning to merge on free. O(total) per operation and the alignment rules are easy to violate.
guide.approach: **Dry run**, total 16. `alloc 3` → need 4; only a 16 is free → split into 8+8 (upper 8 at address 8 freed), then 4+4 (address 4 freed) → return 0. `alloc 2` → need 2; smallest free block ≥ 2 is the 4 at address 4 → split, free `[6,8)`, return 4. `free 0` → size 4, buddy `0^4 = 4` is not in `free[4]` (it was split) → stays 4. `alloc 8` → block at 8. `free 4` → size 2, buddy 6 is free → merge to (4, size 4); buddy `4^4 = 0` is free → merge to (0, size 8); buddy 8 is allocated → stop, return 8. `free 8` → merges with 0 → 16.
guide.complexity: Each operation walks at most log₂(total) levels. Finding the lowest address with `min` on a set is linear in that set; use a heap or sorted structure per level for strict O(log) bounds.
guide.pitfalls: Computing the buddy as `addr + size` (second wrong solution) — only right for the lower half. Never coalescing (first wrong solution), which fragments memory permanently. Merging with a buddy that is only *partly* free: checking membership in `free[size]` at the same size is what prevents that.
guide.follow_up: Measure internal fragmentation: a request for 33 units consumes 64. Slab allocators sit on top of the buddy system to serve small fixed-size objects without that waste.

os-fcfs-scheduling.title: FCFS Scheduling: Waiting and Turnaround
os-fcfs-scheduling.description:
A single CPU runs jobs strictly in order of arrival (first-come, first-served) and never preempts.

`procs[i] = [arrival, burst]` describes job `i` (the index is its id). Jobs that arrive at the same
instant run in increasing id order. If the CPU has nothing to run it sits idle until the next arrival.

Return a list where entry `i` is `[waiting, turnaround]` for job `i`:

- **turnaround** = completion time − arrival time
- **waiting** = turnaround − burst

**Example:** `procs = [[0, 5], [1, 3], [2, 1]]` → `[[0, 5], [4, 7], [6, 7]]`
(job 1 starts at 5 and ends at 8; job 2 runs from 8 to 9).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(procs) ≤ 10^4`, `arrival ≥ 0`, `burst ≥ 1`. The input is *not* guaranteed to be sorted.
os-fcfs-scheduling.solution:
def fcfs(procs):
    order = sorted(range(len(procs)), key=lambda i: (procs[i][0], i))
    res = [None] * len(procs)
    clock = 0
    for i in order:
        arrival, burst = procs[i]
        clock = max(clock, arrival) + burst
        res[i] = [clock - arrival - burst, clock - arrival]
    return res

guide.prereqs: The scheduling lesson: arrival time, burst time, turnaround and waiting time. Sorting with a key.
guide.intuition: FCFS is a single queue at a ticket counter. The only state you need is one clock: the moment the CPU next becomes free. Each job starts at the later of *its arrival* and *that clock*.
hints: Process the jobs in arrival order, but remember where each answer belongs: the output is indexed by the original job id.
Keep a variable `clock`. A job starts at `max(clock, arrival)` — the `max` covers idle gaps.
After a job finishes at `clock`, turnaround is `clock - arrival` and waiting is that minus the burst.
guide.brute_force: Advance a clock one time unit at a time, keeping an explicit queue of arrived jobs. It works, but costs O(total time) instead of O(n log n) and adds nothing for a non-preemptive policy.
guide.approach:
1. Build a list of job ids sorted by `(arrival, id)`.
2. Walk it with `clock = 0`. For each job: `clock = max(clock, arrival) + burst`.
3. Store `[clock - arrival - burst, clock - arrival]` at the job's original index.

**Dry run** on `[[4,2],[0,6],[2,1]]`: order is job 1, job 2, job 0.
Job 1: clock = max(0,0)+6 = 6 → wait 0, turnaround 6.
Job 2: clock = max(6,2)+1 = 7 → wait 4, turnaround 5.
Job 0: clock = max(7,4)+2 = 9 → wait 3, turnaround 5.
Answer `[[3,5],[0,6],[4,5]]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep. Space O(n) for the order and the result.
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting the idle gap (`clock += burst` only) produces negative waiting times. Returning results in arrival order instead of id order. Breaking arrival ties arbitrarily — the statement fixes them by id.
guide.follow_up: Compute the average waiting time and observe the *convoy effect*: put one long job first and watch every short job behind it suffer.

os-sjf-scheduling.title: Shortest Job First (Non-preemptive)
os-sjf-scheduling.description:
Simulate **non-preemptive shortest-job-first** on one CPU.

`procs[i] = [arrival, burst]`. Whenever the CPU becomes free, it picks, among the jobs that have
already arrived, the one with the smallest burst. Ties are broken by earlier arrival, then by smaller id.
Once started, a job runs to completion. If nothing has arrived, the CPU idles until the next arrival.

Return `[[waiting, turnaround], ...]` indexed by job id.

**Example:** `procs = [[0, 7], [1, 2], [2, 4], [3, 1]]` → `[[0, 7], [7, 9], [8, 12], [4, 5]]`
(run order: job 0, job 3, job 1, job 2).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(procs) ≤ 10^4`, `burst ≥ 1`.
os-sjf-scheduling.solution:
import heapq

def sjf(procs):
    n = len(procs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (procs[i][0], i))
    res = [None] * n
    ready, clock, k = [], 0, 0
    while k < n or ready:
        if not ready and procs[order[k]][0] > clock:
            clock = procs[order[k]][0]
        while k < n and procs[order[k]][0] <= clock:
            i = order[k]
            heapq.heappush(ready, (procs[i][1], procs[i][0], i))
            k += 1
        burst, arrival, i = heapq.heappop(ready)
        clock += burst
        res[i] = [clock - arrival - burst, clock - arrival]
    return res

guide.prereqs: FCFS simulation (previous problem), heaps / priority queues, the scheduling lesson's argument that shortest-first minimises mean turnaround.
guide.intuition: The decision point is *the moment the CPU becomes free*. Only jobs that already exist can compete, so you need two structures: a list of future arrivals sorted by time, and a min-heap of ready jobs keyed by burst.
hints: Sorting everything by burst is wrong: a short job that has not arrived yet cannot be chosen.
Maintain a pointer into the arrival-sorted list. Each time the clock moves, push every job with `arrival <= clock` into a heap.
Heap key `(burst, arrival, id)` implements all three tie-break levels at once. If the heap is empty, jump the clock to the next arrival.
guide.brute_force: At each decision scan every unfinished job, filter those that have arrived, and take the minimum: O(n) per decision, O(n²) overall. Perfectly fine for small n and a good way to check a heap solution.
guide.approach:
1. Sort ids by `(arrival, id)`; set `clock = 0`.
2. Loop while jobs remain: if the heap is empty, jump `clock` to the next arrival. Push all arrived jobs.
3. Pop the smallest `(burst, arrival, id)`, advance the clock by its burst, record the result.

**Dry run** `[[0,7],[1,2],[2,4],[3,1]]`: at t=0 only job 0 is ready → runs to 7. At t=7 the heap holds bursts 2, 4, 1 → job 3 runs 7–8 (wait 4), job 1 runs 8–10 (wait 7), job 2 runs 10–14 (wait 8).
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n): one sort plus one push and one pop per job. Space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Sorting globally by burst (ignores arrivals). Forgetting to idle when the ready set is empty. Pushing arrivals only *before* jumping the clock, which leaves the heap empty and crashes on pop.
guide.follow_up: Real systems do not know bursts in advance; they estimate them with exponential averaging of past bursts. Try feeding this simulator estimated bursts instead of true ones.

os-srtf-scheduling.title: Shortest Remaining Time First (Preemptive)
os-srtf-scheduling.description:
Simulate **shortest-remaining-time-first**, the preemptive version of SJF.

`procs[i] = [arrival, burst]`. At every instant the CPU runs the arrived, unfinished job with the least
*remaining* time. Ties: earlier arrival first, then smaller id. Consequently a newly arrived job
preempts the running one only when its burst is **strictly** smaller than the running job's remaining time.

Return `[[waiting, turnaround], ...]` indexed by job id, where waiting = turnaround − burst.

**Example:** `procs = [[0, 8], [1, 4], [2, 2]]` → `[[6, 14], [2, 6], [0, 2]]`
(timeline: job 0 for 0–1, job 1 for 1–2, job 2 for 2–4, job 1 for 4–7, job 0 for 7–14).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(procs) ≤ 10^4`, `burst ≥ 1`, times up to `10^9` (do not step one tick at a time).
os-srtf-scheduling.solution:
import heapq

def srtf(procs):
    n = len(procs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (procs[i][0], i))
    done = [0] * n
    ready, clock, k, finished = [], 0, 0, 0
    while finished < n:
        while k < n and procs[order[k]][0] <= clock:
            i = order[k]
            heapq.heappush(ready, (procs[i][1], procs[i][0], i))
            k += 1
        if not ready:
            clock = procs[order[k]][0]
            continue
        rem, arrival, i = heapq.heappop(ready)
        nxt = procs[order[k]][0] if k < n else float("inf")
        run = min(rem, nxt - clock)
        clock += run
        if rem == run:
            done[i] = clock
            finished += 1
        else:
            heapq.heappush(ready, (rem - run, arrival, i))
    return [[done[i] - a - b, done[i] - a] for i, (a, b) in enumerate(procs)]

guide.prereqs: Non-preemptive SJF, heaps, event-driven simulation (jumping between interesting instants instead of ticking).
guide.intuition: The schedule can only change at two kinds of instants: a job arrives, or the running job finishes. Between two such events the choice is fixed, so run the current best job until whichever event comes first.
hints: Keep a heap of `(remaining, arrival, id)` for ready jobs and a pointer into the arrival-sorted list.
Pop the best job and let it run for `min(remaining, next_arrival - clock)` time units.
If it did not finish, push it back with its reduced remaining time. The heap then decides whether the newcomer preempts it.
guide.brute_force: Tick one unit at a time, choosing the minimum-remaining job each tick. O(total time × n) — hopeless when a burst is 10⁹, but an excellent oracle for small random tests.
guide.approach:
1. Sort ids by arrival. `clock = 0`.
2. Push all jobs with `arrival <= clock`. If none are ready, jump to the next arrival.
3. Pop the minimum; compute `run = min(rem, next_arrival - clock)`; advance the clock.
4. Finished → record completion. Otherwise push back `(rem - run, arrival, id)`.

**Dry run** `[[0,8],[1,4],[2,2]]`: t=0 job 0 runs 1 unit (rem 7). t=1 heap {(7,j0),(4,j1)} → j1 runs 1 unit (rem 3). t=2 heap {(7,j0),(3,j1),(2,j2)} → j2 runs 2, done at 4. j1 runs 3, done at 7. j0 runs 7, done at 14.
guide.complexity: The loop body runs at most 2n times (each iteration either finishes a job or consumes an arrival), so O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Preempting on ties (causes useless context switches and different answers). Ticking unit by unit and timing out. Computing waiting as `start - arrival`, which is wrong once a job can be interrupted — use `turnaround - burst`.
guide.follow_up: Count context switches, then add a switch cost and see when SRTF stops beating SJF.

os-round-robin.title: Round Robin: Build the Gantt Chart
os-round-robin.description:
Simulate **round-robin** scheduling with time slice `quantum` and return the Gantt chart.

`procs[i] = [arrival, burst]`. The ready queue is FIFO. The job at the head runs for
`min(quantum, remaining)` time units. When its slice ends:

1. every job that arrived **during or exactly at the end of** the slice joins the queue (by arrival, then id),
2. *then* the job that just ran rejoins the tail if it still has work left.

If the queue is empty the CPU idles until the next arrival.

Return a list of slices `[id, start, end]` in execution order. Do **not** merge consecutive slices of the same job.

**Example:** `procs = [[0, 5], [1, 3]], quantum = 2` →
`[[0,0,2],[1,2,4],[0,4,6],[1,6,7],[0,7,8]]`

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(procs) ≤ 2000`, `burst ≥ 1`, `quantum ≥ 1`.
os-round-robin.solution:
from collections import deque

def round_robin(procs, quantum):
    n = len(procs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (procs[i][0], i))
    rem = [b for _, b in procs]
    queue, out = deque(), []
    clock = k = 0
    while k < n or queue:
        if not queue:
            clock = max(clock, procs[order[k]][0])
        while k < n and procs[order[k]][0] <= clock:
            queue.append(order[k])
            k += 1
        i = queue.popleft()
        run = min(quantum, rem[i])
        out.append([i, clock, clock + run])
        clock += run
        rem[i] -= run
        while k < n and procs[order[k]][0] <= clock:
            queue.append(order[k])
            k += 1
        if rem[i]:
            queue.append(i)
    return out

guide.prereqs: Queues (`collections.deque`), FCFS simulation, the idea of a time quantum.
guide.intuition: Round robin is FCFS with a timer. The entire subtlety is the *order of two enqueues* at the end of a slice: newcomers first, the preempted job second. Get that order right and everything else is bookkeeping.
hints: Keep arrivals in a sorted list with a pointer, and the ready jobs in a deque.
After advancing the clock past a slice, admit every job with `arrival <= clock` before deciding what to do with the job that just ran.
If the deque is empty but jobs remain, jump the clock forward to the next arrival instead of looping.
guide.brute_force: Tick one time unit at a time with a per-job counter of how much of the quantum has been used. Correct but O(total burst) steps with fiddly state; the slice-at-a-time version is both shorter and faster.
guide.approach:
1. `clock = 0`, pointer `k = 0` into arrival order, empty deque.
2. If the deque is empty, set `clock` to the next arrival. Admit all arrived jobs.
3. Pop the head, run `min(quantum, rem)`, append `[id, clock, clock+run]`, advance the clock.
4. Admit arrivals with `arrival <= clock`, then re-append the job if unfinished.

**Dry run** `[[0,3],[2,1],[2,1]]`, q=2: slice `[0,0,2]`; at t=2 jobs 1 and 2 arrive and enter *before* job 0 → queue [1,2,0]. Slices `[1,2,3]`, `[2,3,4]`, `[0,4,5]`.
guide.complexity: The number of slices is S = Σ⌈burst/quantum⌉. Time O(n log n + S), space O(n + S) for the output.
guide.pitfalls: Re-queuing the preempted job before admitting newcomers. Seeding the queue with all jobs regardless of arrival. Merging adjacent slices when the statement says not to. Infinite loop when the queue is empty and you forget to jump the clock.
guide.follow_up: Derive waiting times from the chart. Then plot average turnaround against the quantum: very small quanta drown in switches, very large ones degenerate into FCFS.

os-priority-scheduling.title: Preemptive Priority Scheduling
os-priority-scheduling.description:
Simulate **preemptive priority scheduling**.

`procs[i] = [arrival, burst, priority]`, and a **smaller number means higher priority**. At every instant
the CPU runs the arrived, unfinished job with the best priority; among equals the one that arrived
earlier wins, then the smaller id (so equal-priority jobs are served FCFS, with no time slicing).
A newcomer preempts only if its priority is strictly better.

Return `[[waiting, turnaround], ...]` indexed by job id.

**Example:** `procs = [[0, 5, 2], [1, 2, 0], [2, 3, 2]]` → `[[2, 7], [0, 2], [5, 8]]`
(job 0 runs 0–1, job 1 preempts for 1–3, job 0 resumes 3–7, job 2 runs 7–10).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(procs) ≤ 10^4`, `burst ≥ 1`, times up to `10^9`.
os-priority-scheduling.solution:
import heapq

def priority_schedule(procs):
    n = len(procs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (procs[i][0], i))
    rem = [p[1] for p in procs]
    done = [0] * n
    ready, clock, k, finished = [], 0, 0, 0
    while finished < n:
        while k < n and procs[order[k]][0] <= clock:
            i = order[k]
            heapq.heappush(ready, (procs[i][2], procs[i][0], i))
            k += 1
        if not ready:
            clock = procs[order[k]][0]
            continue
        prio, arrival, i = ready[0]
        nxt = procs[order[k]][0] if k < n else float("inf")
        run = min(rem[i], nxt - clock)
        clock += run
        rem[i] -= run
        if rem[i] == 0:
            heapq.heappop(ready)
            done[i] = clock
            finished += 1
    return [[done[i] - p[0] - p[1], done[i] - p[0]] for i, p in enumerate(procs)]

guide.prereqs: SRTF simulation (the structure is identical), heaps with tuple keys.
guide.intuition: Replace *remaining time* in SRTF with a fixed priority number. Because the key of a job never changes while it runs, you can leave it at the top of the heap and only pop it when it finishes.
hints: The heap key is `(priority, arrival, id)`; none of these change over time.
Peek at the top, run it until it finishes or until the next arrival, whichever is sooner.
After the next arrival is pushed, simply peek again — if the newcomer is better it is now on top, which *is* the preemption.
guide.brute_force: Unit-time ticking, scanning all jobs each tick for the best arrived one: O(T·n). Useful as a checker on tiny inputs only.
guide.approach:
1. Sort ids by arrival; keep `rem[i]`.
2. Admit arrivals up to `clock`; if none ready, jump the clock.
3. Peek the best job; `run = min(rem, next_arrival - clock)`; update clock and rem; pop only when rem hits zero.

**Dry run** `[[0,5,2],[1,2,0],[2,3,2]]`: job 0 runs 0–1 (rem 4). Job 1 (prio 0) arrives, tops the heap, runs 1–2, then job 2 arrives (prio 2, not better), job 1 finishes at 3. Top is job 0 (earlier arrival than job 2) → 3–7. Job 2 → 7–10.
guide.complexity: O(n log n) time — each job is pushed and popped once, and the loop body runs at most 2n times. O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Reversing the priority convention. Rotating equal-priority jobs (that is priority + round robin, a different policy). Forgetting that a low-priority job may wait forever in a real system — *starvation* — which is why real schedulers add aging.
guide.follow_up: Add aging: every T time units a waiting job's priority number drops by one. How does the worst-case wait change?

os-mlfq.title: Multilevel Feedback Queue
os-mlfq.description:
Simulate a simplified **multilevel feedback queue** (MLFQ).

There are `len(quanta)` FIFO queues; level 0 is the highest priority and level `L-1` the lowest.
`quanta[l]` is the time slice used at level `l`. `procs[i] = [arrival, burst]`.

Rules:

- A newly arrived job enters level 0.
- The scheduler always takes the head of the highest-priority non-empty queue and runs it for
  `min(quanta[level], remaining)` time units. Slices are **not** interrupted by arrivals (decisions happen only at slice boundaries).
- At the end of a slice, first admit every job with `arrival <= now` to level 0 (by arrival, then id).
  Then, if the job that ran is unfinished, it is demoted to the next lower level (the bottom level
  feeds back into itself, giving round robin there).
- If all queues are empty, the CPU idles until the next arrival.

Return the list of completion times indexed by job id.

**Example:** `procs = [[0, 6], [0, 2]], quanta = [2, 4]` → `[8, 4]`
(job 0 runs 0–2 and is demoted; job 1 runs 2–4 and finishes; job 0 runs 4–8 at level 1).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(procs) ≤ 2000`, `1 ≤ len(quanta) ≤ 8`, all quanta and bursts `≥ 1`.
os-mlfq.solution:
from collections import deque

def mlfq(procs, quanta):
    n, levels = len(procs), len(quanta)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (procs[i][0], i))
    rem = [b for _, b in procs]
    done = [0] * n
    queues = [deque() for _ in range(levels)]
    clock = k = 0
    left = n
    while left:
        while k < n and procs[order[k]][0] <= clock:
            queues[0].append(order[k])
            k += 1
        lvl = next((l for l in range(levels) if queues[l]), None)
        if lvl is None:
            clock = procs[order[k]][0]
            continue
        i = queues[lvl].popleft()
        run = min(quanta[lvl], rem[i])
        clock += run
        rem[i] -= run
        while k < n and procs[order[k]][0] <= clock:
            queues[0].append(order[k])
            k += 1
        if rem[i] == 0:
            done[i] = clock
            left -= 1
        else:
            queues[min(lvl + 1, levels - 1)].append(i)
    return done

guide.prereqs: Round-robin simulation, the scheduling lesson's discussion of multiple queues and why CPU-bound jobs sink.
guide.intuition: MLFQ learns a job's nature by watching it. A job that burns a whole slice looks CPU-bound and is pushed down to a level with longer but rarer slices; short interactive jobs finish near the top. The simulation is round robin with an array of queues instead of one.
hints: Use a list of deques. Picking the next job is a scan for the first non-empty level.
Reuse the round-robin skeleton: admit arrivals, run one slice, admit arrivals again, then demote or retire.
The demotion target is `min(level + 1, L - 1)`; the clamp is what makes the last level a round robin.
guide.brute_force: Tick-by-tick simulation with per-job 'slice used so far' counters. It handles the rules but is slower and far easier to get wrong at slice boundaries.
guide.approach:
1. Sort ids by arrival; create `L` deques; `clock = 0`.
2. Admit arrivals to level 0. Find the highest non-empty level; if none, jump the clock.
3. Run the head for `min(quanta[level], rem)`. Admit arrivals up to the new clock.
4. Finished → record. Otherwise append to `min(level+1, L-1)`.

**Dry run** `[[0,10],[3,1]]`, quanta `[2,4,8]`: job 0 runs 0–2 → level 1. Level 0 empty, so job 0 runs 2–6 at level 1 (job 1 arrives at 3 but cannot interrupt) → level 2. Job 1 runs 6–7, done. Job 0 runs 7–11, done. Answer `[11, 7]`.
guide.complexity: Each slice costs O(L) to find a queue. With S slices in total: O(n log n + S·L) time, O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Putting the demoted job back in the same level. Forgetting that the bottom level recycles. Skipping the second 'admit arrivals' step, which lets a demoted job jump ahead in the single-level case. Preempting mid-slice when the statement forbids it.
guide.follow_up: Real MLFQs add a periodic *priority boost* that moves everything back to level 0 to prevent starvation and to forgive jobs whose behaviour changed. Add a boost every B time units.

os-disk-fcfs.title: Disk Scheduling: FCFS Head Movement
os-disk-fcfs.description:
A disk arm starts at cylinder `head`. Pending requests are served strictly in the order given.
Return the total number of cylinders the arm travels.

**Example:** `head = 53, requests = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67]` → `640`

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(requests) ≤ 10^5`, cylinders are non-negative integers.

guide.prereqs: The disk lesson: cylinders, seek time, why arm movement dominates on rotating disks.
guide.intuition: Seek distance is just the absolute difference between consecutive positions. FCFS does no reordering, so the answer is the length of the path head → r₀ → r₁ → …
hints: Walk the list keeping the current arm position.
Add `abs(next - current)` and then move.
The empty list costs nothing.
guide.brute_force: Move the arm one cylinder at a time towards each target, counting steps. O(total distance) instead of O(n).
guide.complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.
guide.pitfalls: Measuring every request from the *original* head position (first wrong solution). Assuming the answer is the span between the extremes (second wrong solution) — that is only a lower bound.
guide.follow_up: Use this as the baseline when you implement SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN and LOOK in the next problems.

os-disk-sstf.title: Disk Scheduling: Shortest Seek Time First
os-disk-sstf.description:
With **SSTF**, the arm always serves the pending request closest to its current position. When two
pending requests are equally close, serve the one on the **lower-numbered** cylinder.

Return the total head movement, starting from cylinder `head`.

**Example:** `head = 53, requests = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67]` → `236`
(order 65, 67, 37, 14, 98, 122, 124, 183).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ len(requests) ≤ 2·10^4`; duplicates allowed.

guide.prereqs: FCFS disk scheduling, binary search (`bisect`), greedy algorithms.
guide.intuition: SSTF is 'shortest job first' for the disk arm: do the cheapest thing next. In a sorted list of pending cylinders the nearest one is always an immediate neighbour of the head position, so you never need to look further than two candidates.
hints: The nearest request must be re-evaluated after every move — sorting once by distance from the *initial* head is wrong.
Sort the cylinders. `bisect_left` gives the insertion point; the candidates are the elements just left and just right of it.
Use `<=` when comparing left distance to right distance so that ties go to the lower cylinder.
guide.brute_force: Each round, scan all pending requests for the minimum `(distance, cylinder)` and remove it: O(n²). Easy to trust; use it to validate the bisect version.
guide.complexity: O(n log n) for sorting plus n binary searches; `list.pop` in the middle is O(n), so O(n²) worst case in pure Python — a balanced tree or two-pointer expansion gives true O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls: Sorting once by initial distance (first wrong solution). Breaking ties upward (second wrong solution). Forgetting that SSTF can **starve** far-away requests when new ones keep arriving near the arm.
guide.follow_up: Because the pending set is static here, the arm's visited range only ever grows outward: implement it with two pointers expanding from the head position and no deletions.

os-disk-scan.title: Disk Scheduling: SCAN (Elevator to the Edge)
os-disk-scan.description:
In this version of **SCAN** the arm sweeps in its current direction serving every request it passes.

- If no pending request lies on the other side of the starting position, the arm stops at the last request in its direction.
- Otherwise it continues **all the way to the edge** of the disk (cylinder `max_cyl` when moving `"up"`,
  cylinder `0` when moving `"down"`), reverses, and serves the remaining requests, stopping at the last one.

Requests on the starting cylinder cost nothing. Return the total head movement.

**Example:** `head = 53, requests = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67], max_cyl = 199, direction = "down"`
→ `236` (53 → 0 is 53 cylinders, then 0 → 183 is 183).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ head, requests[i] ≤ max_cyl`, `len(requests) ≤ 10^5`.
os-disk-scan.starter:
def disk_scan(head, requests, max_cyl, direction):
    pass

guide.prereqs: FCFS and SSTF disk scheduling. The lift analogy from the disk lesson.
guide.intuition: A sweep visits every cylinder between its endpoints, so you never need to simulate individual requests: the total is determined by where the arm turns round and where it finally stops. Only three numbers matter — the head, the edge, and the farthest request on the far side.
hints: Split the requests into those below the head and those above it; requests *at* the head are free.
Moving up with nothing below: the arm just goes to the highest request.
Moving up with something below: it travels `max_cyl - head` to the edge, then `max_cyl - min(below)` back down.
guide.brute_force: Sort the requests, build the explicit visiting order (upward part, edge, downward part) and sum absolute differences as in FCFS. O(n log n) and a good cross-check for the closed form.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** head 53 moving down, queue `98 183 37 122 14 124 65 67`, max 199: above = {98,183,122,124,65,67} is non-empty, so the arm goes to cylinder 0 (53) and then up to the largest request 183 (183). Total 236.
Moving up instead: `(199 − 53) + (199 − 14) = 146 + 185 = 331`.
guide.complexity: O(n) time (one pass for min/max), O(n) or O(1) space depending on whether you build the two lists.
guide.pitfalls: Reversing at the last request instead of the edge — that is LOOK (first wrong solution). Going to the edge even when nothing is waiting behind (second wrong solution; the statement says the arm stops). Counting requests at the head position as movement.
guide.follow_up: SCAN favours the middle cylinders, which are passed twice per round trip. C-SCAN (next problem) evens out the waiting time.

os-disk-cscan.title: Disk Scheduling: C-SCAN
os-disk-cscan.description:
**Circular SCAN** serves requests only while moving **upwards**.

- Starting at `head`, the arm moves up serving every request at or above its position.
- If requests below the starting position remain, the arm continues to the top edge `max_cyl`,
  flies back to cylinder `0` without serving anything (that return trip **counts** as `max_cyl` cylinders
  of movement), and then moves up again to the largest of the remaining requests.
- If nothing lies below the starting position, the arm simply stops at the highest request.

Return the total head movement.

**Example:** `head = 53, requests = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67], max_cyl = 199` → `382`
(146 up to the edge, 199 for the return, 37 up to the last request).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ head, requests[i] ≤ max_cyl`, `len(requests) ≤ 10^5`.

guide.prereqs: SCAN disk scheduling (previous problem).
guide.intuition: Treat the cylinders as a ring: after the top edge comes cylinder 0. The arm keeps travelling the same way round the ring, so a request never waits for more than one full lap — unlike SCAN, where a request just behind the arm waits for almost two sweeps.
hints: Again only the extremes matter: split into below and above the head.
If nothing is below, there is no wrap-around at all.
With a wrap: up to the edge, the full-width return, then up to the **largest** of the below-requests (it is served last on the second pass).
guide.brute_force: Sort, build the visiting order `above ascending → max_cyl → 0 → below ascending` and add up the absolute differences.
guide.approach: **Dry run** head 53, max 199: below = {37, 14}. Up to the edge: 199 − 53 = 146. Return: 199. Up to max(below) = 37. Total 382.
guide.complexity: O(n) time.
guide.pitfalls: Using `min(below)` as in SCAN's formula (first wrong solution) — on the second pass the arm moves upward, so it ends at the *largest* low request. Forgetting to count the return seek (second wrong solution); some textbooks exclude it, so always check the convention you are asked for.
guide.follow_up: C-LOOK jumps from the highest request straight to the lowest one instead of visiting both edges. Write its closed form.

os-disk-look.title: Disk Scheduling: LOOK Service Order
os-disk-look.description:
**LOOK** is the elevator algorithm that reverses at the last request rather than at the disk edge.

Starting at cylinder `head` and moving in `direction` (`"up"` or `"down"`):

1. requests located exactly at `head` are served first;
2. then every request ahead of the arm, in the order the arm reaches them;
3. then the arm reverses and serves the rest.

Duplicate requests are all served when the arm reaches that cylinder. Return the order in which the
cylinders are served (a list with the same length as `requests`).

**Example:** `head = 53, requests = [98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67], direction = "up"`
→ `[65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, 37, 14]`

**Constraints:** `len(requests) ≤ 10^5`.

guide.prereqs: SCAN and C-SCAN, sorting with `reverse=True`.
guide.intuition: An elevator serves floors in one direction in increasing distance, then turns round and does the same the other way. So the answer is two sorted runs glued together: ascending for the upward leg, descending for the downward leg.
hints: Partition the requests into three groups: at the head, above, below.
Above must be ascending; below must be **descending** — in both directions of travel that is the order the arm meets them.
Concatenate according to the starting direction.
guide.brute_force: Simulate the arm cylinder by cylinder, emitting requests as it passes them and reversing when nothing remains ahead. O(range of cylinders) rather than O(n log n).
guide.approach: **Dry run** head 53, up: above sorted `[65,67,98,122,124,183]`; below descending `[37,14]`. Order: 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, 37, 14. Movement would be (183−53) + (183−14) = 299, versus 331 for SCAN to the edge.
guide.complexity: O(n log n) time for the two sorts, O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Leaving the lower group ascending (first wrong solution) — the arm would have to jump to the far end first, which is C-LOOK, not LOOK. Ordering by distance from the start (second wrong solution) is a zig-zag no real arm would perform.
guide.follow_up: Compute the total movement from the order and compare LOOK, SCAN, C-SCAN, SSTF and FCFS on the same queue. On SSDs none of this matters: there is no arm, so Linux uses a no-op style scheduler.

os-inode-max-file-size.title: Maximum File Size of an Inode
os-inode-max-file-size.description:
A UNIX-style inode contains `direct` direct block pointers, plus `single` single-indirect, `double`
double-indirect and `triple` triple-indirect pointers. Blocks are `block_size` bytes and a block
pointer occupies `ptr_size` bytes, so one indirect block holds `block_size // ptr_size` pointers.

Return the largest file size in **bytes** that the pointer structure can address.

**Example:** `block_size = 1024, ptr_size = 4, direct = 10, single = 1, double = 1, triple = 0`
→ pointers per block = 256 → `(10 + 256 + 256²) × 1024 = 67,383,296`

**Constraints:** `block_size` and `ptr_size` are powers of two with `ptr_size ≤ block_size`; counts are `≥ 0`.
os-inode-max-file-size.starter:
def max_file_size(block_size, ptr_size, direct, single, double, triple):
    pass
os-inode-max-file-size.solution:
def max_file_size(block_size, ptr_size, direct, single, double, triple):
    n = block_size // ptr_size
    blocks = direct + single * n + double * n ** 2 + triple * n ** 3
    return blocks * block_size

guide.prereqs: The file-system implementation lesson: inodes, direct and indirect blocks.
guide.intuition: Count data blocks, then multiply by the block size. Each level of indirection multiplies reach by the fan-out `n = block_size / ptr_size`: a single-indirect pointer reaches `n` blocks, a double `n²`, a triple `n³`.
hints: First compute how many pointers fit in one block.
A double-indirect pointer leads to a block of `n` pointers, each leading to a block of `n` data pointers.
Sum the reachable data blocks over all pointer kinds and convert to bytes at the very end.
guide.brute_force: Recursively 'walk' the tree and count leaves. Pointless for a triple-indirect tree with a billion leaves; the closed form is the only sensible approach.
guide.approach:
`blocks = direct + single·n + double·n² + triple·n³`, answer `blocks × block_size`.

**Dry run** 4 KB blocks, 4-byte pointers: n = 1024. Blocks = 12 + 1024 + 1,048,576 + 1,073,741,824 = 1,074,791,436 → about 4.4 × 10¹² bytes (≈ 4 TiB).
guide.pitfalls: Multiplying by the level number instead of raising to a power (first wrong solution). Using the block size as the fan-out (second). Returning blocks instead of bytes (third). In real systems the limit may be lower still because the file-size field or the block-pointer width (e.g. 32 bits) caps it first.
guide.follow_up: How many disk reads are needed to fetch byte 5,000,000 of a file if only the inode is cached? See the next problem.

os-inode-block-lookup.title: Inode Block Lookup Path
os-inode-block-lookup.description:
An inode has `direct` direct pointers followed by one single-indirect, one double-indirect and one
triple-indirect pointer. Every indirect block holds `n` pointers.

Given a file's **logical block number** `block_no` (0-based), return the path used to find it:

- `[0, i]` — direct pointer `i`
- `[1, i]` — entry `i` of the single-indirect block
- `[2, i, j]` — entry `i` of the double-indirect block, then entry `j` of that block
- `[3, i, j, k]` — the analogous three indices under the triple-indirect pointer
- `[]` — the block number is beyond what the inode can address

**Example:** `block_no = 300, direct = 12, n = 256` → `[2, 0, 32]`
(blocks 0–11 are direct, 12–267 single-indirect; 300 − 268 = 32 → first second-level block, slot 32).

**Constraints:** `0 ≤ block_no < 2^62`, `0 ≤ direct ≤ 64`, `1 ≤ n ≤ 2^16`.

guide.prereqs: Inode structure (previous problem), integer division and remainder as 'digit extraction'.
guide.intuition: The inode lays its regions end to end: direct, then single, double, triple. Subtract the sizes of the regions you skip; what is left is an index *inside* the region, and writing that index in base `n` gives the slot to follow at each level.
hints: Handle the regions in order, subtracting each region's capacity before testing the next.
Inside the double-indirect region the remaining index `b` splits as `(b // n, b % n)`.
Inside the triple region the three digits are `b // n²`, `(b // n) % n`, `b % n`.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate logical blocks from 0, advancing a multi-level odometer until you reach `block_no`. O(block_no) — unusable for a block number near 10⁹.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `block_no = 1036`, 12 direct, n = 1024: not direct; b = 1024; not `< 1024`, so subtract → b = 0 → `[2, 0, 0]`, the very first block reached through the double-indirect pointer.

For `[3, i, j, k]` each lookup costs four block reads beyond the inode: three pointer blocks plus the data block.
guide.complexity: O(1) time and space.
guide.pitfalls: Not subtracting earlier regions (first wrong solution). Off-by-one boundaries with `<=` (second wrong solution) — the block at index `direct` is the first single-indirect one. Forgetting the 'too large' case.
guide.follow_up: Extent-based file systems (ext4, NTFS, XFS) replace this pointer tree with (start, length) runs. What does the lookup become?

os-fat-chain.title: Follow a FAT Chain
os-fat-chain.description:
In a FAT file system the table `fat` has one entry per disk block: `fat[b]` is the number of the next
block of the same file, or `-1` if `b` is the file's last block.

Given the table and a file's first block `start` (or `-1` for an empty file), return the list of the
file's blocks in order.

A damaged table may contain an entry pointing outside the table or a chain that loops back on itself.
In either case return `None`.

**Example:** `fat = [-1, -1, 10, 11, 7, -1, 3, 2, -1, -1, 12, 14, -1, -1, -1], start = 4`
→ `[4, 7, 2, 10, 12]`

**Constraints:** `len(fat) ≤ 10^6`.

guide.prereqs: Linked-list allocation with an in-memory table (file-system implementation lesson).
guide.intuition: The FAT is a linked list whose 'next' pointers have been pulled out of the data blocks into one array. Reading a file's block list is therefore a pointer chase through that array — plus the paranoia any on-disk structure deserves.
hints: Loop: append the current block, then jump to `fat[current]`, until you read `-1`.
Before using a block number as an index, check it is within `0 .. len(fat) - 1`.
A loop in the chain would run forever; remember visited blocks in a set.
guide.brute_force: Detect loops by comparing against every block already in the list (`b in chain`): O(length²). A set makes it O(length).
guide.approach:
**Dry run** start 4: `fat[4] = 7`, `fat[7] = 2`, `fat[2] = 10`, `fat[10] = 12`, `fat[12] = -1` → `[4,7,2,10,12]`.
Corrupt case `fat = [1, 0]`, start 0: visit 0, then 1, then 0 again → already seen → `None`.
guide.complexity: O(length of chain) time and space.
guide.pitfalls: No cycle check (infinite loop) or a check that silently returns a truncated list instead of signalling corruption (first wrong solution). Wrapping bad indices instead of rejecting them (second). Treating `start = -1` as an error — it is a legitimate empty file.
guide.follow_up: Random access to block k of a file costs k steps in the chain, but all in RAM. The price is the table itself: one entry per disk block must stay in memory, which is why FAT does not scale to huge volumes.

os-raid-parity.title: RAID Parity and Reconstruction
os-raid-parity.description:
A RAID level 4/5 stripe consists of data blocks plus one parity block, where the parity is the
bytewise XOR of all the data blocks. Each block is a list of byte values (0–255) of equal length.

`stripe` is a list of blocks.

- If exactly one entry is `None`, that drive has failed: return the reconstructed block (it may be a
  data block or the parity block — the computation is the same).
- If no entry is `None`, the list holds only data blocks: return their parity block.

**Example:** `stripe = [[1, 2, 3], None, [7, 7, 7]]` → `[6, 5, 4]`

**Constraints:** 1 to 64 blocks, block length up to 4096, at most one `None`. A stripe consisting only of `None` reconstructs to an empty block `[]`.

guide.prereqs: XOR and its properties; RAID levels (disk lesson).
guide.intuition: XOR is its own inverse: `a ^ b ^ b = a`. If `P = D0 ^ D1 ^ D2`, then XOR-ing P with any two of the data blocks cancels them and leaves the third. So 'compute parity' and 'rebuild a missing block' are the *same* operation: XOR everything you still have.
hints: Ignore the `None` entry and combine the others.
Work column by column: byte `i` of the result is the XOR of byte `i` of every surviving block.
Start the accumulator at 0, the identity for XOR.
guide.brute_force: For each byte position try all 256 candidate values and keep the one that makes the XOR of the whole column zero. It works because exactly one value fits — and shows why parity can repair one loss but not two.
guide.approach: **Dry run** `[[1,2,3], None, [7,7,7]]`: column 0: 1 ^ 7 = 6; column 1: 2 ^ 7 = 5; column 2: 3 ^ 7 = 4 → `[6,5,4]`. Check: `[1,2,3] ^ [6,5,4] = [7,7,7]`, consistent whichever of the three is called 'parity'.
guide.complexity: O(blocks × block length) time, O(block length) space.
guide.pitfalls: Using addition modulo 256 (first wrong solution) — rebuilding would then need subtraction, and the parity/data symmetry is lost. Using OR (second), which destroys information. Forgetting that single parity survives only one failure; a second failure, or an unreadable sector found during the rebuild, loses data, which motivates RAID 6.
guide.follow_up: A small write need not read the whole stripe: `new_parity = old_parity ^ old_data ^ new_data`. Implement that update and verify it against a full recomputation.

os-free-bitmap.title: Free-space Bitmap: Find a Run of Free Blocks
os-free-bitmap.description:
A file system tracks free blocks with a bitmap stored as a list of bytes. Block `i` is described by
bit `i % 8` of byte `i // 8`, counting from the **least significant** bit; a `1` bit means *in use*.

Return the number of the first block that starts a run of at least `n` consecutive free blocks, or
`-1` if there is no such run. The disk has exactly `8 * len(bitmap)` blocks.

**Example:** `bitmap = [0b00001111, 0b11111000], n = 5` → `4`
(blocks 0–3 used, 4–10 free, 11–15 used).

**Constraints:** `len(bitmap) ≤ 10^5`, `1 ≤ n ≤ 10^6`.

guide.prereqs: Bit operations; free-space management with bitmaps versus free lists (memory and file-system lessons).
guide.intuition: Flatten the bytes into one long row of bits and look for the first stretch of `n` zeros. A single counter of 'zeros seen since the last one' is all the state required; the bit ordering inside a byte is the only real trap.
hints: Bit `k` of a byte is `(byte >> k) & 1`.
Keep `run`; reset it on a used block, increment on a free one, and return as soon as it reaches `n`.
The run started at `current_block - n + 1`. Runs may cross byte boundaries, so never reset between bytes.
guide.brute_force: For every starting block test the next `n` bits: O(blocks × n). Fine for tiny disks, quadratic for large runs.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** bytes `00001111`, `11111000`, n = 5: blocks 0–3 used (run 0). Blocks 4, 5, 6, 7 free → run 4. Block 8 is bit 0 of the second byte = 0 → run 5 → start = 8 − 5 + 1 = 4.

Optional speed-up used in the reference: a byte equal to 0 adds 8 to the run at once when that cannot yet complete it.
guide.complexity: O(number of blocks) time, O(1) space.
guide.pitfalls: Reading bits most-significant first (first wrong solution). Resetting the counter at each byte (second) — contiguous runs spanning bytes are then missed. Returning the *end* of the run.
guide.follow_up: Real allocators scan a word at a time (find-first-zero instructions) and keep per-group free counts so that full regions are skipped entirely — the idea behind ext2/ext4 block groups.

os-unix-permissions.title: UNIX Permission Check
os-unix-permissions.description:
Decide whether a process may access a file under the classic UNIX nine-bit permission model.

- `mode` — the permission bits as an integer (e.g. `0o640` = `rw-r-----`)
- `owner`, `group` — the file's owner uid and group gid
- `uid`, `gids` — the process's effective uid and the list of groups it belongs to
- `want` — a non-empty string made of the letters `r`, `w`, `x`: **all** listed rights are required

Rules:

1. Exactly **one** class applies: if `uid == owner` use the owner bits; otherwise if `group` is in
   `gids` use the group bits; otherwise use the "other" bits. There is no fall-through to a more generous class.
2. The superuser (`uid == 0`) may always read and write; it may execute only if at least one of the three execute bits is set.

Return `True` or `False`.

**Example:** `mode = 0o640, owner = 1000, group = 50, uid = 1001, gids = [50], want = "r"` → `True`;
with `want = "rw"` → `False`.
os-unix-permissions.starter:
def can_access(mode, owner, group, uid, gids, want):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Octal notation, bit masks, the protection-domain discussion in the security and Linux lessons.
guide.intuition: The mode is three 3-bit groups — owner, group, other. The kernel first decides *who you are relative to the file* and then looks at only that group. The surprising consequence: an owner can be locked out of a file everyone else can read.
hints: Extract a class with a shift and a mask: owner `(mode >> 6) & 7`, group `(mode >> 3) & 7`, other `mode & 7`.
Use `if / elif / else` to choose the class, so that exactly one applies.
Handle uid 0 first; note the special treatment of execute.
guide.brute_force: Render the mode as the string `rwxr-x---` and index into it. Perfectly valid and arguably clearer; the bit version is what the kernel does.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `0o640`, owner 1000, group 50. Process uid 1001 in group 50 → group class → bits `100` → read only. `"r"` → True; `"rw"` → False.
`0o077` with the owner asking for `r`: owner class is `000` → False, even though group and other have everything.
guide.complexity: O(len(want)) time, O(1) space.
guide.pitfalls: OR-ing the classes together (first wrong solution). Letting root execute a file with no execute bit at all (second). Requiring *any* rather than *all* requested rights (third). Masking: bits above the low nine (setuid, setgid, sticky) must not disturb the result.
guide.follow_up: Real systems layer more on top: access control lists, capabilities such as `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` instead of an all-powerful uid 0, and mandatory access control (SELinux, AppArmor).

os-bankers-safe-sequence.title: Banker's Algorithm: Find a Safe Sequence
os-bankers-safe-sequence.description:
A system has `m` resource types and `n` processes.

- `available[j]` — free instances of resource `j` right now
- `allocation[i][j]` — instances of `j` currently held by process `i`
- `maximum[i][j]` — the most instances of `j` process `i` may ever hold (its declared claim)

The state is **safe** if the processes can be ordered so that each one, in turn, can obtain its whole
remaining need (`maximum − allocation`) from what is available plus everything released by the
processes before it, then finish and release its allocation.

Return **any** safe sequence as a list of process indices, or `[]` if the state is unsafe.
(Any valid ordering is accepted.)

**Example:** `available = [3, 3, 2]`,
`allocation = [[0,1,0],[2,0,0],[3,0,2],[2,1,1],[0,0,2]]`,
`maximum = [[7,5,3],[3,2,2],[9,0,2],[2,2,2],[4,3,3]]` → e.g. `[1, 3, 4, 0, 2]`

**Constraints:** `1 ≤ n ≤ 200`, `1 ≤ m ≤ 20`, `allocation[i][j] ≤ maximum[i][j]`.
os-bankers-safe-sequence.solution:
def safe_sequence(available, allocation, maximum):
    n = len(allocation)
    work = list(available)
    need = [[mx - al for mx, al in zip(maximum[i], allocation[i])] for i in range(n)]
    done = [False] * n
    seq = []
    progress = True
    while progress:
        progress = False
        for i in range(n):
            if not done[i] and all(x <= w for x, w in zip(need[i], work)):
                work = [w + a for w, a in zip(work, allocation[i])]
                done[i] = True
                seq.append(i)
                progress = True
    return seq if len(seq) == n else []

guide.prereqs: The deadlock-avoidance lesson: safe and unsafe states, the Need matrix. Basic list comprehension skills.
guide.intuition: Imagine a cautious banker with limited cash. A customer is 'serviceable' if the banker could hand over *everything* the customer might still ask for. Service that customer in your head, collect their whole loan back, and the vault only grows — so greedily picking any serviceable process never hurts.
hints: Compute `need[i][j] = maximum[i][j] - allocation[i][j]` first.
Keep a `work` vector, starting as `available`. Find any unfinished process whose need fits componentwise inside `work`.
When a process 'finishes', add its *allocation* (not its need) to `work`. Repeat until no process can be added; safe iff all are done.
guide.brute_force: Try all n! orderings and test each one. Correct, and a fine oracle for n ≤ 8, but the greedy search is polynomial because the order in which serviceable processes are picked cannot turn a safe state into a stuck one.
guide.complexity: At most n passes over n processes, each comparing m numbers: O(n²·m) time, O(n·m) space.
guide.pitfalls: Releasing `need` instead of `allocation`, or releasing nothing (second wrong solution). Making a single pass in index order (third wrong solution) — a process skipped early may become serviceable later. Comparing only the sum of needs rather than each resource type.
guide.follow_up: To decide whether to *grant* a request, pretend to grant it (move units from available to allocation), run this check, and roll back if the result is unsafe.

os-deadlock-detection.title: Deadlock Detection on a Resource Graph
os-deadlock-detection.description:
Every resource has a single instance.

- `holds[r]` is the process currently holding resource `r`, or `-1` if it is free.
- `wants[p]` is the one resource process `p` is blocked waiting for, or `-1` if `p` is not waiting.

A process waiting for a free resource is not stuck (the resource will simply be granted). A process is
**deadlocked** if it can never run again: it is part of a circular wait, or it is waiting — directly or
through a chain of other waiting processes — for a process that is part of one.

Return the sorted list of deadlocked processes.

**Example:** `holds = [0, 1, 2], wants = [1, 0, 0, -1]` → `[0, 1, 2]`
(P0 and P1 wait for each other; P2 holds R2 and waits for R0, held by P0, so it is stuck behind the cycle; P3 is fine).

**Constraints:** up to `10^5` processes and resources. A process may wait for a resource it holds itself (a self-deadlock).

guide.prereqs: Resource-allocation graphs and the four deadlock conditions (deadlock lesson). Cycle detection in a functional graph.
guide.intuition: Collapse the resource graph into a *wait-for* graph: P → Q when P waits for something Q holds. Each process has at most one outgoing edge, so following edges from any process traces a single path that either ends (someone runnable — the whole chain will eventually drain) or loops (everyone on the path is stuck forever).
hints: Define `next(p)`: `-1` if `p` wants nothing or wants a free resource, else `holds[wants[p]]`.
Walk from each unvisited process, marking nodes 'on the current path'. Stop when you hit `-1`, a node on the current path, or a node already classified.
Whatever verdict the stopping point has, the entire path inherits it. Hitting your own path means a new cycle was found.
guide.brute_force: From every process follow the chain for up to n steps; if it has not terminated by then, it must be looping, so the start is deadlocked. O(n²) in the worst case (one long chain), but obviously correct.
guide.approach:
Three-colour walk with path labelling.

**Dry run** `holds=[0,1,2]`, `wants=[1,0,0,-1]`: start P0 → wants R1 held by P1 → P1 wants R0 held by P0, which is on the current path → cycle: P0, P1 deadlocked. Start P2 → wants R0 held by P0, already 'deadlocked' → P2 inherits it. P3 wants nothing → fine. Answer `[0,1,2]`.
guide.complexity: Every process is put on a path exactly once: O(n) time, O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Reporting only the processes *on* the cycle and missing those queued behind it (first wrong solution). Treating every blocked process as deadlocked (second wrong solution) — blocking is normal; only unresolvable waiting is deadlock. Forgetting the self-wait case.
guide.follow_up: With several instances per resource a cycle is necessary but not sufficient; you then need the matrix-based detection algorithm from the lesson, which is the banker's safety check run on current requests instead of maximum claims.

os-dining-philosophers.title: Dining Philosophers: Replay a Schedule
os-dining-philosophers.description:
`n ≥ 2` philosophers sit round a table; fork `i` lies between philosopher `i` and philosopher `i-1`,
so philosopher `p` uses forks `p` and `(p + 1) % n`.

Each philosopher picks up a **first** fork and then a **second** fork:

- if `ordered` is `False`: first = fork `p`, second = fork `(p + 1) % n`;
- if `ordered` is `True` (resource ordering): first = the lower-numbered of the two, second = the higher.
