`schedule` is the sequence in which the philosophers get a turn. On its turn, philosopher `p` does exactly one thing:

- holding no fork → takes the first fork if it is free (otherwise nothing happens);
- holding one fork → takes the second fork if it is free (otherwise nothing happens);
- holding both → eats, then puts both forks down (one meal).

Return `[meals, deadlock]` where `meals[p]` counts philosopher `p`'s meals and `deadlock` is `True`
when, after the schedule, **every** philosopher holds exactly one fork.

**Example:** `n = 3, schedule = [0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2], ordered = False` → `[[0, 0, 0], True]`

**Constraints:** `2 ≤ n ≤ 1000`, `len(schedule) ≤ 10^5`.

guide.prereqs: The classic-IPC lesson (dining philosophers), the circular-wait condition, and resource ordering as a prevention technique.
guide.intuition: Threads are just interleavings. Fix the interleaving as data and a concurrency puzzle becomes an ordinary state machine: each philosopher is in state 0, 1 or 2 (forks held) and each turn advances that machine by at most one step.
hints: Track `owner[fork]` and `held[p]`.
Compute `(first, second)` at the top of each turn; with `ordered` swap them when `first > second` — that only ever happens for the last philosopher.
Deadlock here is simply `all(h == 1 for h in held)`: n forks, n holders, each waiting for a neighbour.
guide.brute_force: There is no asymptotically worse sensible approach — the simulation is the specification. A real-thread version would be *non-deterministic*, which is exactly why we replay a schedule instead.
guide.approach:
**Dry run**, n=3, unordered, schedule `0 1 2 0 1 2`: P0 takes fork 0, P1 takes fork 1, P2 takes fork 2. Second round: P0 wants fork 1 (held by P1), P1 wants fork 2, P2 wants fork 0 — nobody moves. Everyone holds one fork → deadlock.

Ordered: P2's forks are {2, 0}, so its first fork is 0, already taken by P0 → P2 holds nothing. Then P0 wants fork 1 (held), P1 takes fork 2 and can eat on its next turn. No circular wait can form.
guide.complexity: O(len(schedule)) time, O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls: Ignoring the `ordered` flag (first wrong solution). Letting a philosopher grab a fork that is already owned (second wrong solution) — the mutual-exclusion violation the whole problem is about. Counting a meal when the second fork is picked up rather than on the following turn.
guide.follow_up: Other cures: allow at most n−1 philosophers to reach for forks at once (a counting semaphore), or pick up both forks atomically inside a monitor.

os-readers-writers.title: Readers–Writers Lock Simulation
os-readers-writers.description:
Simulate a readers–writers lock. `requests[i] = [arrival, kind, duration]` with `kind` `"R"` or `"W"`.
Any number of readers may hold the lock together; a writer needs it exclusively. A request that starts
at time `s` holds the lock during `[s, s + duration)`.

At every instant where something arrives or finishes, do in order: (1) release finished holders,
(2) add new arrivals to the waiting list (by arrival, then index), (3) admit according to `prefer`:

- `"readers"`: if no writer is active, **all** waiting readers start (even if writers are waiting).
  Then, if nobody holds the lock, the earliest waiting writer starts.
- `"writers"`: if any writer is waiting, readers are held back; the earliest waiting writer starts as
  soon as nobody holds the lock. If no writer is waiting and none is active, all waiting readers start.

Return the list of start times indexed by request.

**Example:** `requests = [[0,"R",4],[1,"W",2],[2,"R",4]]`
- `prefer = "readers"` → `[0, 6, 2]` (the second reader slips in; the writer waits until 6)
- `prefer = "writers"` → `[0, 4, 6]`

**Constraints:** up to 2000 requests, `duration ≥ 1`.

guide.prereqs: The readers–writers problem from the classic-IPC lesson; event-driven simulation as used in the SRTF problem.
guide.intuition: The lock has only three interesting states: free, held by k readers, held by one writer. Policy matters at exactly one point — when both a reader and a writer are waiting and the lock could admit readers. 'Readers first' maximises concurrency and can starve writers; 'writers first' keeps data fresh and can starve readers.
hints: Keep `reader_ends` (finish times of active readers), `writer_end` (or None) and a `waiting` list in arrival order.
Write one `admit` step that is called at every event time after releasing finished holders and enqueuing arrivals.
The next event time is the minimum of the next arrival and — only if someone is waiting — the earliest finish among current holders.
guide.brute_force: Advance time one unit at a time and run the same release / enqueue / admit steps on every tick. Easier to reason about and a good cross-check, at O(total time) cost.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `[[0,R,4],[1,W,2],[2,R,4]]`.
*Readers preference*: t=0 R0 starts (ends 4). t=1 W1 waits. t=2 R2 arrives; no writer active → starts (ends 6). t=4 R0 leaves; a reader is still active. t=6 lock free → W1 starts. Result `[0,6,2]`.
*Writers preference*: t=2 R2 arrives but a writer is waiting → held back. t=4 lock free → W1 starts (ends 6). t=6 R2 starts. Result `[0,4,6]`.
guide.complexity: O(E · n) with E events for this straightforward version (the waiting list is rescanned at each event); heaps and separate reader/writer queues bring it to O(n log n).
guide.pitfalls: Serialising everything as if it were a plain mutex (first wrong solution). Ignoring the policy flag (second wrong solution). Letting a writer start while readers are still inside. Advancing time to a holder's finish when nobody is waiting, which is harmless but can loop forever if you never break.
guide.follow_up: Design a *fair* policy: a single FIFO queue where a batch of consecutive readers enters together. Neither side can starve.

os-semaphore-trace.title: Evaluate a Semaphore Trace
os-semaphore-trace.description:
A counting semaphore starts with value `initial ≥ 0` and has a FIFO queue of blocked processes.
`ops` is a list of `[pid, op]` pairs executed in order, where `op` is `"P"` (down / wait) or `"V"` (up / signal).

- `P`: if the value is positive, decrement it; otherwise the caller blocks and joins the queue.
- `V`: if the queue is non-empty, wake the process at its head (the value stays unchanged — the
  woken process consumes the signal); otherwise increment the value.
- An operation issued by a process that is currently blocked is **ignored** (a blocked process cannot run).

Return `[value, blocked, woken]`: the final value, the pids still blocked in queue order, and the pids
that were woken, in wake-up order.

**Example:** `initial = 1, ops = [[1,"P"],[2,"P"],[3,"P"],[1,"V"],[2,"V"]]` → `[0, [], [2, 3]]`

**Constraints:** up to `10^5` operations.

guide.prereqs: Semaphores (down/up, also written P/V or wait/signal) from the IPC lesson; queues.
guide.intuition: A semaphore is a counter of 'permits' plus a waiting room. `P` takes a permit or sits down to wait; `V` hands a permit directly to the first waiter if there is one, and only otherwise returns it to the counter. Value and queue are never both non-zero.
hints: Maintain the integer value, a FIFO queue, and a set of blocked pids for fast membership tests.
On `V` with waiters, do **not** increment: the permit is passed straight to the woken process.
Skip any operation whose pid is in the blocked set.
guide.brute_force: A plain list with `pop(0)` and `pid in list` checks is O(n) per operation — O(n²) for a long trace with many blocked processes. A deque and a set fix both.
guide.approach: **Dry run** `initial=1`: P by 1 → value 0. P by 2 → blocks, queue [2]. P by 3 → blocks, queue [2,3]. V by 1 → wakes 2, queue [3], value still 0. V by 2 (now runnable) → wakes 3. Result `[0, [], [2,3]]`.
guide.complexity: O(len(ops)) time, O(number of blocked processes) space.
guide.pitfalls: Incrementing on every `V` (first wrong solution) lets a later `P` steal a permit that was already given away. Executing operations of blocked processes (second wrong solution). Using a stack instead of a queue, which starves early waiters.
guide.follow_up: Some textbooks let the value go negative, with `-value` equal to the number of waiters. Rewrite the function in that convention and show both give the same wake-up order.
